newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European Q4 refining margins expected up from 1995.
newsitem.headline: European Q4 refining margins expected up from 1995.

text.p: The tremendous strides made by middle distillates in the last month should push fourth quarter refining margins above those of last year, although the rally may not last much beyond early November, analysts say.

"The fourth quarter will start on a strong note because of (the strength of) middle distillates, but there is a threat as to how long the middle distillate rally can continued," said Peter Bogin, associate director at oil consultants Cambridge Energy Research Associates.
Margins in the third quarter were up on last year with a sizeable contribution from September's gas oil prices.
"September was way above average. The gas oil crack has been between $50 and $60 (a tonne). Anything above $50 is normally considered exceptional," said a Dutch refining economist.
The result has been a third quarter margin improvement of about 10-15 cents a barrel over 1995.

Analysts expect margins in the fourth quarter to be similar to those of the third and so higher than last year, but if cold weather arrives earlier than normal, there is scope for even greater improvement.
"Our projection is (of margins) about 25 cents better (than Q4 1995), but the upside could be 50 cents better," said an economist at a European major.
Colin Birch, principal consultant at Purvin and Gertz, makes a distinction between margins for catalytic cracking and hydrocracking.
The yield of better quality gas oil, more suitable for higher priced diesel and jet fuel, from the latter process means the hydrocracking margins will be better.
"For cat cracking, Q4 will be fairly similar to last year, a bit better, but not a lot...The hydrocracker margin will be considerably higher," Birch said.

However, margins are heavily reliant on middle distillate strength, which analysts say is bound to wane as the fourth quarter unfolds and consumer stocks steadily rise. There is little incentive for consumers to build inventories, beyond what is essential, at these high prices, they say.
"We eventually think this (middle distillate) rally will ease off, probably in early or mid-November," Bogin said.
If and when gas oil does fade, there is little prospect of margins recovering since the products at the ends of the barrel are relatively weak.
"There will be no gasoline support in the fourth quarter and only modest improvement in the fuel oil outlook," Bogin said.
Analysts say the margin for fuel oil averaged $2 less in the third quarter than in the fourth.
One thing, however, that seems sure to lift margins is the introduction this autumn of low sulphur diesel.
Since refiners are seeking to recoup their outlay on desulphurisation units, the prices will be higher than for the higher sulphur diesel in production last year.
"Diesel now costs about $8 a tonne more than gas oil and only costs about $4 extra to produce, although, of course, that extra is needed to cover the capital costs," said Birch.
